intro: Marcelle Meyer plays the Gavotte et six doubles from the Suite in A minor in Rameau’s Nouvelles Suites de pièces de clavecin, on the piano. The gavotte theme is followed by six variations, in which quick runs pass from one hand to the other.

sections.label: Theme · Gavotte in A minor
sections.mNote: Two repeated halves, ornamented with trills and turns.

sections.label: Var 1 · Right-hand running notes
sections.mNote: Quick right-hand notes run above the slower left-hand tune.

sections.label: Var 2 · Running left-hand bass under chords
sections.mNote: Running bass notes support the upper chords.

sections.label: Var 3 · Moving middle voice
sections.mNote: Quick notes move between the held outer parts.

sections.label: Var 4 · Repeated notes in pairs
sections.mNote: Each note of the tune is struck twice in quick succession.

sections.label: Var 5 · Right-hand leaps
sections.mNote: The upper part leaps between low and high registers.

sections.label: Var 6 · Left-hand leaps
sections.mNote: The bass plays the running figures up to the final cadence.

relations.label: The gavotte’s second strain repeats
relations.basis: The gavotte has two repeated strains, the second twice the length of the first. These excerpts lie in that longer strain and its repeat before the first double. CENS diagonal mean 0.957, sustained 25 s, fixed pitch-class shift 0 semitones and time offset 27 s (cache/form/rameau-gavotte-six-doubles.txt, candidate 1; 0.5 s grid). These are matched excerpts, not complete section boundaries; timing has not been checked by ear.

relations.label: The first double repeats its second strain
relations.basis: The first double retains the gavotte’s repeated-strain design while adding upper figuration. These excerpts compare the same strain within that double. CENS diagonal mean 0.975, sustained 16.5 s, fixed pitch-class shift 0 semitones and time offset 19 s (cache/form/rameau-gavotte-six-doubles.txt, candidate 3; 0.5 s grid). These are matched excerpts, not complete section boundaries; timing has not been checked by ear.

relations.label: The harmonic route survives another double
relations.basis: The fifth and sixth doubles preserve the gavotte’s harmonic route while changing the keyboard figuration. The long paired excerpts lie in their later strains; the relation does not claim identical melody or finger-work. CENS diagonal mean 0.929, sustained 26.5 s, fixed pitch-class shift 0 semitones and time offset 50 s (cache/form/rameau-gavotte-six-doubles.txt, candidate 2; 0.5 s grid). These are matched excerpts, not complete section boundaries; timing has not been checked by ear.

cues.title: Gavotte and six doubles
cues.text: The gavotte moves in two broad beats, and trills and small turns ornament its tune. Each half repeats. Rameau keeps these phrases and their cadences through six doubles, variations with progressively busier figuration.
cues.evidence: Rameau, Nouvelles Suites de pièces de clavecin, Saint-Saëns edition (Durand, 1895), pp. 76–81: gavotte and six doubles. https://archive.org/download/imslp-suites-de-pices-de-clavecin-rameau-jean-philippe/Rameau_-_nouvelles_suite.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Move to Paris, 1722
cues.text: In 1722 Rameau moved from Clermont to Paris and published his Traité de l’harmonie. By then he had spent years as a church organist. His first opera at the Paris Opéra, Hippolyte et Aricie, followed in 1733, when he was fifty.
cues.evidence: M. Elizabeth C. Bartlet, Rameau biography in Europe, 1450 to 1789: Encyclopedia of the Early Modern World, on Clermont, Paris, the 1722 treatise and the 1733 Opéra début. https://www.encyclopedia.com/people/literature-and-arts/music-history-composers-and-performers-biographies/jean-philippe-rameau-0

cues.title: First double, right-hand semiquavers
cues.text: In the first double the right hand plays continuous semiquavers above a slower tune in the left hand. The gavotte’s chords fall in their original places, and the semiquavers fill the beats between them.
cues.evidence: Saint-Saëns edition, pp. 76–77, first double: continuous upper semiquavers and slower left-hand notes.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Rameau’s Traité de l’harmonie, 1722
cues.text: In the preface to his Traité de l’harmonie (1722), Rameau declared that “music is a science which must have definite rules”. His central rule was that a chord and its inversions share one root. The basse fondamentale, the imagined line of those roots, was for him the true bass.
cues.evidence: Rameau, Traité de l’harmonie (1722), preface: “La Musique est une science qui doit avoir des regles certaines” (text at https://frances.paginas.ufsc.br/files/2022/06/traite-de-lhmonie-de-rameau.pdf; translation ours). Chord roots, inversions and the fundamental bass: M. Elizabeth C. Bartlet and Baker’s Biographical Dictionary of Musicians, both at https://www.encyclopedia.com/people/literature-and-arts/music-history-composers-and-performers-biographies/jean-philippe-rameau-0

cues.title: Second double, left-hand semiquavers
cues.text: In the second double the hands exchange roles. The left hand plays running semiquavers in broken chords, and the right hand holds the slower notes above.
cues.evidence: Saint-Saëns edition, p. 77, second double: running left-hand semiquavers beneath sustained upper chords.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Third double, inner voice
cues.text: The third double puts quick notes inside the chords. A held upper note and a slower bass surround the moving middle voice.
cues.evidence: Saint-Saëns edition, p. 78, third double: sustained outer notes around the moving inner part.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Fourth double, repeated notes
cues.text: In the fourth double the melody moves in quick pairs of repeated notes, with a few running figures between them. The gavotte’s two broad beats stay the same underneath.
cues.evidence: Saint-Saëns edition, pp. 78–79, fourth double: paired repeated semiquavers within the unchanged duple metre.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Fifth double, right-hand leaps
cues.text: In the fifth double the right hand leaps between separated notes, joined by short semiquaver runs. The bass moves in slower notes beneath. The phrases stay in A minor and cover a much wider span.
cues.evidence: Saint-Saëns edition, pp. 79–80, fifth double: separated upper notes joined by semiquavers, over a slower bass.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Sixth double, left-hand figuration
cues.text: The sixth double gives the running figures to the left hand beneath held right-hand chords. Low and high notes alternate within the bass line. The set ends with this variation’s cadence in A minor.
cues.evidence: Saint-Saëns edition, pp. 80–81, sixth double: left-hand running figures and the final A minor cadence.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: From the gavotte to the first double
transitions.how: The gavotte closes in A minor. The first double begins the same phrases with continuous right-hand semiquavers above slower left-hand notes. On Meyer’s piano the tune now sits beneath the running part, and the two-beat dance metre continues.
transitions.evidence: Saint-Saëns edition, p. 76: the gavotte’s A minor cadence and the first double’s upper semiquavers. https://archive.org/download/imslp-suites-de-pices-de-clavecin-rameau-jean-philippe/Rameau_-_nouvelles_suite.pdf

transitions.title: From the third to the fourth double
transitions.how: The third double ends on a cadence in A minor. The fourth double starts the dance again in pairs of repeated notes, and each pair carries the tune on to the next note. The moving inner voice of the third double is replaced by a succession of quick repeated notes above the bass.
transitions.evidence: Saint-Saëns edition, p. 78: third-double cadence and the opening paired notes of the fourth double. https://archive.org/download/imslp-suites-de-pices-de-clavecin-rameau-jean-philippe/Rameau_-_nouvelles_suite.pdf

composer.epithet: Composer and theorist who explained the roots of chords in a treatise and wrote his first opera at the age of fifty.
facts: Organist in Dijon, Clermont-Ferrand and Lyon; first harpsichord book, 1706
Traité de l’harmonie, 1722; Nouveau système de musique théorique, 1726
Alexandre Le Riche de La Pouplinière, financier with a private orchestra
composer.background:
When Hippolyte et Aricie opened at the Paris Opéra on 1 October 1733, Rameau had just turned fifty. One passage had already been cut. A trio for the Fates, with harmonies that proved too difficult for the singers and players in rehearsal, was removed before the premiere. The opera divided its audience. Admirers heard a new theatrical voice, while devotees of Lully heard an attack on their inheritance. It was the first opera by Rameau, an organist from Dijon.

His father played the organ in Dijon. Jean-Philippe followed the same trade in a succession of French churches, with appointments in Clermont-Ferrand, Dijon and Lyon and an early attempt to establish himself in Paris. There he published his first harpsichord book in 1706. It begins with an unmeasured prelude, in which the player must work out the timing of the notes, followed by a faster section in regular metre. Allemandes, courante and sarabandes follow. He was twenty-three, and he was writing within the French keyboard tradition before Couperin had published his first book.
